idiom_name: val x by lazy { build() } with LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED
implementation_notes: Kotlin owns the pattern through property delegation: kotlin-stdlib's lazy() returns a Lazy<T> delegate whose default SYNCHRONIZED mode computes the value in one thread and publishes it so all threads see the same value, so the null-marker plus lock structure is deleted rather than replaced by a library call at each access - the delegate is the field. Lazy<T> also exposes isInitialized(), and lateinit var covers 'assign later' without a factory. The delegate is write-once, so values that must be rebuilt need a volatile cell or a Deferred instead.
pitfalls: SYNCHRONIZED mode serialises first access: every thread touching the property while the initialiser runs blocks, and an initialiser that reads the same property re-enters the delegate (which is still uninitialised) and recurses.

The delegate is write-once: there is no reset or reload, so configuration-driven values need a separate @Volatile cell or a Deferred - re-shuffling a lazy property's backing field is not part of its contract.

A lazy property participates in implicit work: toString, hashCode, equals, serialisation and framework reflection can all trigger the build at points the author never intended, and a lazy property is not part of a data class's generated members.

variants.name: Confined or recomputation-tolerant lazy delegate
variants.implementation_notes: The thread-safety mode is the tuning knob: LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE drops locking entirely for objects confined to one thread (UI objects, request-scoped state, per-thread workers), and PUBLICATION allows racing threads to compute independently and publishes the first value that finishes, which is useful when recomputation is cheap and blocking is unacceptable. Both keep the delegation syntax and only change the publication policy, which is why this variant exists: the default is not always the right contract.
pitfalls: NONE on a property that is ever touched from another thread is a data race with no compiler diagnostic - the mode is a promise the type system cannot check.
PUBLICATION may execute the initialiser several times (all results but one are discarded), so it must stay side-effect free.
Switching modes during a refactor changes both the cost profile and the failure behaviour of the property, and nothing in the call site hints at which mode is in force.
